questions.q: Explain the transformer architecture at a high level.
questions.answer: A transformer is a stack of identical blocks. Each block has (1) multi-head self-attention, which lets every token mix information from other tokens, and (2) a position-wise feed-forward network (MLP). Residual connections and layer normalization wrap both sub-layers so deep stacks train stably. Most modern LLMs are decoder-only: causal masking means each token attends only to earlier tokens, and the model is trained to predict the next token. Position information comes from positional encodings, today usually rotary embeddings (RoPE).
questions.follow_up: Why do most LLMs use decoder-only instead of encoder-decoder? (One stack, one objective, scales simply and handles generation natively.)

questions.q: What is self-attention and why does it matter?
questions.answer: Each token is projected into a query, key and value. Attention weights are softmax(QK^T / sqrt(d_k)), and the output is the weighted sum of values. It lets any token pull information from any other token in one step, so long-range dependencies do not have to pass through a recurrent bottleneck, and the whole sequence is processed in parallel during training. The cost is O(n^2) in sequence length for compute and for the attention matrix.
questions.follow_up: Why divide by sqrt(d_k)? Without it, dot products grow with dimension, the softmax saturates and gradients vanish.

questions.q: Explain the KV cache and why it matters for inference.
questions.answer: During autoregressive decoding, the keys and values of earlier tokens do not change, so they are stored and reused; each new token computes only its own Q, K, V. This turns per-step attention from recomputing the whole prefix into one pass over cached tensors. The trade-off is memory: per sequence it is roughly 2 x layers x kv_heads x head_dim x tokens x bytes per value, and it often limits batch size and context length more than the weights do. Grouped-query attention, KV quantization and paged allocation (as in vLLM's PagedAttention) exist to shrink or pack it.
questions.follow_up: Estimate KV-cache memory for a 32-layer model, 8 KV heads, head_dim 128, 8k tokens, fp16: 2x32x8x128x8192x2 bytes, about 1 GiB per sequence.

questions.q: Compare pre-training, instruction tuning and preference tuning (RLHF/DPO).
questions.answer: Pre-training: next-token prediction on trillions of tokens; gives knowledge and fluency but not helpful behavior. Instruction tuning (SFT): supervised training on prompt-response pairs so the model follows instructions and a chat format. Preference tuning: trains on comparisons of better vs worse answers. RLHF fits a reward model and optimizes the policy with RL (e.g. PPO) under a KL penalty to the SFT model; DPO skips the reward model and optimizes directly on preference pairs, which is simpler and more stable. Each stage uses far less data than the one before.
questions.follow_up: When would you pick DPO over PPO-style RLHF? (Smaller team, offline preference data, want stability; PPO when you need online exploration or a reusable reward model.)

questions.q: What do scaling laws say, and how do they change decisions?
questions.answer: Loss falls as a smooth power law in parameters, data and compute (Kaplan et al., 2020). The Chinchilla work (Hoffmann et al., 2022) showed that for a fixed training budget, parameters and tokens should grow roughly together, around 20 training tokens per parameter, so many earlier models were undertrained. In practice teams now often train smaller models on far more tokens than compute-optimal because inference cost, not training cost, dominates over the model's life.
questions.follow_up: Why would you deliberately train past the compute-optimal point? (Cheaper serving for a model that will answer billions of requests.)

questions.q: What is tokenization and why does it matter?
questions.answer: Text is split into subword units by algorithms such as BPE or unigram (SentencePiece). It matters because cost, latency and context limits are counted in tokens; token count per word varies by language (many non-English languages need more tokens for the same content); and tokenization explains odd failures such as weak character counting, arithmetic on long numbers and sensitivity to leading spaces.
questions.follow_up: Why can an LLM fail to count the letters in a word? (It sees tokens, not characters.)

questions.q: What is the context window and how does it affect system design?
questions.answer: It is the maximum number of tokens (prompt plus output) the model can attend to. Larger windows allow whole documents in the prompt but increase cost and latency, and models use information unevenly across long inputs (relevant facts in the middle are used less reliably). Design still needs retrieval, summarization or memory to choose what goes in, plus a token budget per section (system, history, retrieved context, output).

questions.q: What do temperature and top-p do, and how do you choose them?
questions.answer: Temperature rescales logits before softmax: low values make output near-deterministic, high values flatten the distribution. Top-p (nucleus) sampling keeps only the smallest set of tokens whose cumulative probability reaches p. Use low temperature (0 to 0.3) for extraction, classification and code; moderate (0.7 to 1.0) for brainstorming or creative text. Even at temperature 0, outputs can vary slightly across runs because of batching and floating-point effects, so do not rely on it for strict determinism.

questions.q: Fine-tuning vs in-context learning: what is the difference?
questions.answer: In-context learning puts instructions and examples in the prompt; the weights do not change, iteration is instant, but every request pays for the extra tokens and behavior is bounded by the window. Fine-tuning changes the weights with training examples; it is good for consistent format, tone, a narrow task or making a smaller model as good as a bigger prompted one, but it needs data, evaluation and redeployment, and it is a poor way to add frequently changing facts (use retrieval for that).

questions.q: What is quantization and why is it important for deployment?
questions.answer: Storing weights (and sometimes activations or the KV cache) in fewer bits, e.g. 8-bit or 4-bit integers instead of 16-bit floats. It cuts memory roughly 2x to 4x and often raises throughput because decoding is memory-bandwidth bound. Post-training methods such as GPTQ and AWQ keep quality loss small at 4-bit for many models, but you must re-run your task evals because degradation is uneven (math, code and long context tend to suffer first).

questions.q: Explain LoRA and QLoRA.
questions.answer: LoRA freezes the base weights and learns a low-rank update for selected matrices: W + BA, where A and B have small rank r (often 8 to 64). Trainable parameters drop by orders of magnitude, adapters are small files, and several adapters can share one base model. QLoRA (Dettmers et al., 2023) keeps the frozen base in 4-bit and trains LoRA adapters on top, making fine-tuning of large models feasible on a single GPU.
questions.follow_up: Which layers do you apply LoRA to? (Attention projections at minimum; adding MLP layers usually helps quality at more cost.)

questions.q: Explain Mixture of Experts and its trade-offs.
questions.answer: An MoE layer replaces one feed-forward block with many experts plus a router that sends each token to the top-k experts (often k = 2). Total parameters are large but active parameters per token are small, so quality per training FLOP improves. Costs: all experts must still sit in memory, routing needs load-balancing losses, expert parallelism adds communication, and batching is less efficient at low traffic.

questions.q: How do reasoning models differ from standard chat models?
questions.answer: Reasoning models are trained, typically with reinforcement learning on verifiable tasks, to produce a long internal chain of thought before the final answer, and they spend more inference-time compute per query. They are stronger on math, code and multi-step planning but slower and more expensive, and often worse value for simple lookups or style tasks. In a product, route only hard queries to them and set a reasoning budget.

questions.q: Why do LLMs hallucinate, and how do you reduce it?
questions.answer: The model is trained to produce plausible continuations, not to verify facts, and it has no built-in signal for what it does not know. Reduce it by grounding answers in retrieved sources and asking for citations, allowing and rewarding an "I don't know" path, constraining outputs (schemas, enumerations), lowering temperature for factual tasks, and checking claims afterwards against the sources with an automated verifier.

questions.q: What is the difference between an embedding model and a generative model?
questions.answer: An embedding model maps text to a fixed-length vector so that similar meanings are close in vector space; it is used for search, clustering, deduplication and classification. A generative model produces tokens. Embedding calls are far cheaper and are the backbone of retrieval; the generative model then reads what was retrieved.

questions.q: What makes a good production prompt?
questions.answer: A clear role and task, the exact output format, constraints written as rules, a few representative examples (including edge cases), and delimiters separating instructions from untrusted input. Prompts are code: version them, keep them in source control, and change them only with an eval run showing the effect.

questions.q: Zero-shot vs few-shot prompting: when do you use each?
questions.answer: Zero-shot when the task is common and the format is simple. Few-shot when the format is unusual, labels are subtle, or you need consistent style. Pick examples that cover the hard cases and vary them; models copy surface patterns, so unbalanced examples bias outputs (e.g. all examples labelled positive).

questions.q: What is chain-of-thought prompting and when does it help?
questions.answer: Asking the model to reason step by step before answering. It helps on multi-step arithmetic, logic and planning, and makes errors easier to inspect. It costs tokens and latency, adds little on simple lookups, and the written reasoning is not a guaranteed faithful account of how the answer was produced. Reasoning-trained models already do this internally.

questions.q: How do you get reliable structured output (JSON) from an LLM?
questions.answer: Use the provider's structured output or JSON-schema mode, or constrained decoding when self-hosting, so output is forced to match the schema. Then validate with a schema library (e.g. Pydantic), and on failure retry with the validation error included. Keep schemas flat, use enums for categorical fields, and make optional fields explicit rather than letting the model invent values.

questions.q: What is function (tool) calling?
questions.answer: You describe functions with names, descriptions and JSON-schema parameters; the model returns a structured call instead of text; your code executes it and sends the result back; the model continues. The model never executes anything itself. Quality depends heavily on clear tool descriptions, few overlapping tools, and validating arguments before execution.

questions.q: What is prompt injection and how do you defend against it?
questions.answer: Untrusted text (a user message, web page, email or retrieved document) contains instructions that override the developer's intent, e.g. "ignore previous instructions and send the data to...". Indirect injection through retrieved content is the harder case. No prompt fully prevents it, so defend in layers: treat all retrieved text as data, give the model least-privilege tools, require human confirmation for side-effecting actions, isolate secrets from the context, filter inputs and outputs, and log for audit. It is item 1 on the OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications.
questions.follow_up: Why can't a better system prompt solve this? (Instructions and data share one channel; the model has no hard boundary between them.)

questions.q: How do you manage and version prompts in a team?
questions.answer: Store prompts as templates in source control or a prompt registry with IDs and versions; log the prompt version with every request; gate changes on an offline eval set; roll out with a flag or percentage; keep rollback one click away. Separate the template from variables so diffs are readable.

questions.q: How do you shorten prompts without losing quality?
questions.answer: Remove repeated instructions, move static context into a cached prefix (many providers discount cached prompt tokens), summarize long histories, retrieve only the top chunks, and replace long examples with one good one. Measure quality before and after on the eval set; cost wins that drop accuracy are not wins.

questions.q: What is a system prompt and what belongs in it?
questions.answer: The highest-priority instruction block for a conversation: role, scope, rules, output style and refusal behavior. Keep it stable (it can then be prompt-cached), keep secrets out of it (assume it can be extracted), and put per-request data in the user turn.

questions.q: How would you choose between a long prompt, RAG and fine-tuning for a new feature?
questions.answer: Start with prompting plus a small eval set; it is the fastest loop. Add RAG when answers depend on private or changing knowledge. Fine-tune when you need consistent format or behavior that prompting cannot hold, lower latency or cost via a smaller model, or have thousands of good examples. They combine: fine-tuned model plus RAG is common.

questions.q: Explain the RAG architecture end to end.
questions.answer: Indexing: parse documents, split into chunks, embed each chunk, store vectors with metadata (source, date, permissions). Query time: optionally rewrite the query, embed it, retrieve top-k by vector and/or keyword search, apply metadata filters, re-rank, then put the best chunks in the prompt with instructions to answer only from them and cite sources. Evaluate retrieval and generation separately.
questions.follow_up: Where does RAG usually fail first? (Retrieval: wrong chunk or missing chunk, not the generator.)

questions.q: How do you choose a chunking strategy?
questions.answer: Follow document structure (headings, paragraphs, code blocks, table rows) rather than fixed character counts; typical chunk sizes are a few hundred tokens with modest overlap. Small chunks give precise matches but lose context; large chunks keep context but dilute similarity and cost more tokens. A common fix is to retrieve small chunks and pass their parent section to the model. Choose by measuring recall on real questions, not by default settings.

questions.q: What is hybrid search and when should you use it?
questions.answer: Combining lexical search (BM25) with dense vector search, then merging results, often with reciprocal rank fusion. Use it when queries contain exact identifiers, product codes, names, error messages or rare terms that embeddings blur. It is a sensible default for enterprise search.

questions.q: How does re-ranking work and why use it?
questions.answer: Retrieve a wide candidate set cheaply (e.g. top 50), then score each query-document pair with a cross-encoder or LLM that reads both together, and keep the top 5 to 10. Cross-encoders are more accurate than comparing two independently computed embeddings but too slow to run over the whole corpus, so they are used only on candidates.

questions.q: What is the "lost in the middle" problem?
questions.answer: Liu et al. (2023) found that models use relevant information placed at the start or end of a long context more reliably than information in the middle. Mitigations: retrieve fewer, better chunks; put the most relevant first; re-rank; and test long-context behavior on your own tasks rather than trusting the advertised window.

questions.q: How do you evaluate a RAG system?
questions.answer: Separately. Retrieval: recall@k, precision@k, MRR or nDCG against labelled question-to-source pairs. Generation: faithfulness (claims supported by retrieved context), answer relevance, correctness against a reference, and citation accuracy. Build a golden set from real user questions, use an LLM judge calibrated against human labels, and track latency and cost per answer.

questions.q: How do you keep a RAG index fresh when documents change?
questions.answer: Incremental ingestion keyed by document ID and content hash; re-embed only changed chunks; delete chunks of removed documents (stale chunks are a common source of wrong answers); store timestamps and versions as metadata and filter or boost by recency. Re-embed everything when you change the embedding model, because vectors from different models are not comparable.

questions.q: How should a RAG system decide to say "I don't know"?
questions.answer: Combine signals: low retrieval scores or re-ranker scores below a calibrated threshold, no chunk that answers the question, and a verifier step that checks the draft answer against sources. Instruct the model explicitly that declining is acceptable and evaluate refusal precision as well as answer accuracy.

questions.q: How do you choose an embedding model?
questions.answer: Benchmark candidates on your own query-document pairs (public leaderboards such as MTEB are a starting point only). Consider language coverage, domain fit, max input length, dimension (storage and speed), cost or hosting, and whether it supports asymmetric query/document modes. Record the model version with the index.

questions.q: Compare common vector store options.
questions.answer: Postgres with pgvector: simplest if you already run Postgres, good to millions of vectors. Managed vector databases (e.g. Pinecone): little operations work, pay per usage. Self-hosted engines (e.g. Qdrant, Weaviate, Milvus): more control, filtering and scale. Search engines (Elasticsearch, OpenSearch) suit hybrid lexical plus vector. Pick on filtering needs, scale, latency, operations capacity and cost, not on hype.

questions.q: What are HNSW and IVF indexes, and what trade-offs do they make?
questions.answer: Both are approximate nearest-neighbor indexes. HNSW builds a layered proximity graph: high recall and low latency but high memory and slower builds. IVF clusters vectors and searches only the nearest clusters: lower memory, tunable via the number of probes, often combined with product quantization. You trade recall for speed and memory; measure recall@k against exact search on a sample.

questions.q: What is query transformation and why does it help?
questions.answer: Rewriting the user query before retrieval: resolving pronouns from chat history, expanding acronyms, splitting a multi-part question into sub-queries, or generating a hypothetical answer and embedding that (HyDE). It helps when user phrasing differs from document phrasing; it adds a model call, so measure whether recall gain justifies the latency.

questions.q: How do you enforce access control in RAG?
questions.answer: Store permission metadata (tenant, groups, document ACL) on every chunk at ingestion and filter at query time inside the retrieval call, before anything reaches the model. Never rely on the prompt to hide documents. Keep ACLs in sync with the source system and test with users who should and should not see each document.

questions.q: What is agentic RAG?
questions.answer: Instead of one retrieve-then-generate pass, the model decides when and what to search, can issue several queries, read results, and search again before answering. It handles multi-hop questions better but costs more and is harder to evaluate; cap the number of steps and log each retrieval.

questions.q: How do you debug poor RAG answer quality?
questions.answer: Trace a failing question: was the right document ingested and parsed correctly, was it chunked sensibly, did it appear in the top-k, was it ranked high enough, was it included in the prompt, and did the model use it? Fix the earliest failing stage. Most issues are parsing, chunking or retrieval, not the generator.

questions.q: What is an AI agent, and how is it different from a chain?
questions.answer: A chain is a fixed sequence of steps defined by the developer. An agent is a loop where the model chooses the next action (which tool to call, with what arguments) based on observations, until it decides the task is done. Agents handle open-ended tasks but are less predictable, so use a fixed workflow when the steps are known.

questions.q: Explain the ReAct pattern.
questions.answer: Reason + Act (Yao et al., 2022): the model alternates between a reasoning step, a tool call, and reading the observation, repeating until it can answer. It grounds reasoning in real tool results. In production you add step limits, structured tool calls instead of parsed text, and error handling for failed tools.

questions.q: What is the Model Context Protocol (MCP)?
questions.answer: An open protocol, introduced in late 2024, that standardizes how applications expose tools, resources and prompts to LLM clients. A server describes its tools once and any MCP-compatible client can use them, instead of a custom integration per app and per model. Security still matters: servers run with real permissions, so authenticate them, scope their access and review what they expose.
questions.follow_up: How is MCP different from plain function calling? (Function calling is the model-side format; MCP is the client-server protocol for discovering and invoking tools across apps.)

questions.q: How do you design good tools for an agent?
questions.answer: Few tools with distinct purposes, clear names and descriptions written for the model, strict typed parameters, informative error messages the model can act on, and outputs trimmed to what is needed. Make side-effecting tools idempotent where possible and separate read tools from write tools so permissions can differ.

questions.q: How do you make agents reliable in production?
questions.answer: Bound them: max steps, timeouts and budget per task; validate every tool argument; retry transient errors with backoff; checkpoint state so long tasks can resume; require human approval for irreversible actions; and log full traces. Evaluate on task-completion suites with realistic tool failures, not only on happy paths.

questions.q: How do you handle memory in agents?
questions.answer: Short-term: the running conversation and scratchpad, trimmed or summarized to fit the window. Long-term: facts or past episodes stored externally (database or vector store) and retrieved when relevant. Write to long-term memory deliberately (what is worth keeping), and let users see or delete stored memories for privacy.

questions.q: Single agent vs multi-agent systems: when is multi-agent worth it?
questions.answer: Multi-agent setups (planner plus workers, or specialist agents) help when sub-tasks are separable, need different tools or prompts, or can run in parallel. They add cost, latency and coordination failures. Start with one agent and good tools; split only when evals show a single agent cannot hold the task.

questions.q: What guardrails do agents need?
questions.answer: Input and output filtering, allow-lists of tools per user role, argument validation, rate and spend limits, sandboxed code execution, human confirmation for actions such as payments, emails or deletes, and treating every tool output as untrusted input (it may contain injected instructions).

questions.q: How do you evaluate an agent?
questions.answer: Task success rate on a fixed suite of realistic tasks with checkable end states, plus step count, cost, latency and error recovery. Inspect trajectories, not only outcomes: a correct final answer reached through a risky tool call is still a failure. Re-run the suite on every model or prompt change.

questions.q: What is planning in an agent and why can it fail?
questions.answer: Breaking a goal into steps before or during execution. It fails when the plan is made without enough information, when the agent does not revise the plan after a failed step, or when errors compound over many steps. Re-planning after each observation and short plans with checkpoints reduce this.

questions.q: How do you run model-generated code safely?
questions.answer: Execute it in an isolated sandbox (container or microVM) with no secrets, restricted network, CPU, memory and time limits, a read-only or scratch filesystem, and resource cleanup after the run. Return only stdout, stderr and declared artifacts to the model.

questions.q: Workflows vs agents: how do you decide?
questions.answer: If you can draw the flowchart, build a workflow (deterministic steps with model calls inside); it is cheaper, testable and predictable. Use an agent when the path depends on intermediate results you cannot enumerate. Many good systems are workflows with one agentic step.

questions.q: When should you fine-tune instead of prompting or RAG?
questions.answer: When you need consistent format or style, a narrow task at lower cost or latency with a smaller model, domain language the base model handles poorly, or behavior that long prompts cannot hold. Not for adding facts that change; use retrieval for those.

questions.q: How do you build a fine-tuning dataset?
questions.answer: Collect real inputs, write or curate high-quality target outputs, deduplicate, remove PII, balance across task types and edge cases, and hold out a test set before training. Quality beats volume: a few thousand clean examples often outperform a large noisy set. Version the dataset with the model.

questions.q: What is catastrophic forgetting and how do you limit it?
questions.answer: Fine-tuning on a narrow set can degrade general abilities the base model had. Limit it with parameter-efficient methods (LoRA), lower learning rates and fewer epochs, mixing in general instruction data, and evaluating on general benchmarks as well as the target task.

questions.q: What is model distillation and when would you use it?
questions.answer: Training a smaller student model to imitate a larger teacher, using the teacher's outputs (or probabilities) on many inputs. Use it to cut latency and cost for a well-defined task after you have proven quality with the large model. Check the provider's terms before training on another model's outputs.

questions.q: Explain DPO in one minute.
questions.answer: Direct Preference Optimization (Rafailov et al., 2023) trains on pairs of chosen and rejected responses with a classification-style loss that increases the likelihood of the chosen response relative to a frozen reference model. It reaches results similar to RLHF without training a separate reward model or running RL, so it is simpler and more stable.

questions.q: How do you evaluate a fine-tuned model before shipping?
questions.answer: Compare against the base model and the prompted baseline on a held-out set of the target task, a general-capability set to catch regressions, safety tests, and side-by-side human or LLM-judge review. Ship only if it wins on the target metric without unacceptable regressions, and canary it with monitoring.

questions.q: What hyperparameters matter most in LoRA fine-tuning?
questions.answer: Learning rate, number of epochs, rank r and alpha (scaling), which modules get adapters, batch size and sequence length. Overfitting usually shows as falling training loss with flat or rising validation loss; stop early and keep the best checkpoint.

questions.q: What is synthetic data and what are its risks?
questions.answer: Training examples generated by models, used to expand coverage or create preference pairs. Risks: copying the generator's errors and style, low diversity, contamination of your eval set, and degradation when models train repeatedly on model-generated data ("model collapse", Shumailov et al.). Mitigate with filtering, human spot checks, mixing in real data and strict eval separation.

questions.q: Why is evaluating LLM applications hard?
questions.answer: Outputs are open-ended, many answers can be correct, quality has several dimensions (correctness, faithfulness, tone, safety), and small prompt or model changes shift behavior unpredictably. That is why teams build task-specific eval sets instead of relying on public benchmarks.

questions.q: How do you build an eval set?
questions.answer: Start from real or realistic inputs, cover common cases, edge cases and known failures, write expected outputs or grading criteria for each, and keep it versioned. Start with 50 to 200 examples and grow it from production failures. Keep a held-out portion that is never used for prompt tuning.

questions.q: How do you make LLM-as-judge reliable?
questions.answer: Give the judge a precise rubric and, where possible, a reference answer; ask for a short justification before the score; use pairwise comparison for subjective quality; swap answer order to control position bias; watch for length and self-preference bias; and calibrate against human labels, reporting agreement. Re-check calibration when the judge model changes.

questions.q: Offline vs online evaluation: what is the difference?
questions.answer: Offline: run a fixed eval set before release to catch regressions. Online: measure live behavior through A/B tests, user feedback, task completion, escalation rates and sampled reviews. Both are needed: offline gates releases, online tells you whether users are actually better off.

questions.q: How do you A/B test an AI feature?
questions.answer: Randomize users (not requests) to variants, define a primary metric tied to user value (task success, retention, resolution rate) plus guardrail metrics (latency, cost, complaints), size the test for the effect you care about, and watch for novelty effects. Keep model, prompt and retrieval changes separable so you know what caused the result.

questions.q: What metrics do you track for a production LLM feature?
questions.answer: Quality (eval scores, user ratings, task success), safety (policy violations, refusals), latency (time to first token, total time at p50/p95/p99), cost (tokens and dollars per request), reliability (error, timeout and retry rates) and usage. Slice them by user segment and model version.

questions.q: What is benchmark contamination and why does it matter?
questions.answer: Test questions from a benchmark leaking into training data, which inflates scores without real capability. It is why public leaderboard results may not predict performance on your task. Use private, recently written eval sets and check for overlap when you fine-tune.

questions.q: How do you evaluate hallucination or faithfulness?
questions.answer: Break the answer into individual claims and check each against the provided sources (with an NLI model or an LLM judge), then report the share of supported claims. Pair it with citation checks: does the cited passage actually contain the claim?

questions.q: What is regression testing for prompts and models?
questions.answer: Running the eval suite automatically in CI on every prompt, model or retrieval change and blocking the change if key metrics drop beyond a threshold. It turns prompt changes into reviewed code changes.

questions.q: How do you choose between two models for a feature?
questions.answer: Run both on your eval set and compare quality, then latency at your expected load, cost per successful task (not per token), context and tooling needs, data and compliance terms, and reliability of the provider. Often a cheaper model plus routing for hard cases wins.

questions.q: Design a customer-support assistant for a SaaS company.
questions.answer: Clarify scope (answer questions, take actions, or both), channels, volume and escalation rules. Components: RAG over help docs and past tickets with permission filters; account tools with read-only defaults and confirmation for changes; conversation memory; intent routing to a cheap model for simple questions; human handoff with full context; evals on resolution accuracy; monitoring of escalation and satisfaction. Discuss failure modes: stale docs, prompt injection through tickets, and wrong refunds.

questions.q: Design an evaluation pipeline for an LLM product.
questions.answer: Versioned eval datasets, a runner that executes prompts/models in parallel with caching, graders (exact match, programmatic checks, calibrated LLM judges, human review queues), result storage per run, dashboards with diffs against the baseline, and CI gates. Feed production failures back into the dataset.

questions.q: Design a model-serving platform.
questions.answer: API gateway with auth, quotas and routing; model servers with continuous batching and paged KV cache (e.g. vLLM or TGI); autoscaling on queue depth and GPU utilization; streaming responses; per-tenant rate limits; health checks and fallbacks to another model or provider; and metrics for time to first token, tokens per second and cost.

questions.q: Design a document-processing (extraction) pipeline.
questions.answer: Ingest, then OCR or layout parsing, classify document type, extract fields with schema-constrained output, validate (types, cross-field rules, totals), score confidence, send low-confidence items to human review, and store with lineage back to the page. Measure field-level accuracy per document type.

questions.q: Design an LLM gateway for a company.
questions.answer: One internal endpoint in front of all providers: authentication, per-team keys and budgets, model routing and fallback, prompt and response logging with PII redaction, caching, rate limiting, usage and cost reporting, and policy enforcement. It gives central control and lets teams switch models without code changes.

questions.q: Design a semantic search engine.
questions.answer: Ingestion and chunking, embeddings, an ANN index with metadata filters, hybrid lexical plus vector retrieval, re-ranking, snippets and highlighting, query understanding (spelling, synonyms), and click and relevance feedback for tuning. Evaluate with nDCG on labelled queries.

questions.q: Design a real-time content moderation system.
questions.answer: Layered: fast rules and hashes for known bad content, a small classifier for most traffic, and an LLM or human review for ambiguous cases; policy defined as labeled categories; latency budget per layer; appeals flow; and monitoring of precision and recall per category and language. Bias and over-blocking are as important as misses.

questions.q: How do you architect a multi-tenant AI platform?
questions.answer: Isolate tenant data at storage and retrieval (tenant ID filters enforced server-side, separate indexes for high-sensitivity tenants), per-tenant keys, quotas and cost tracking, per-tenant prompt or adapter configuration, noisy-neighbor protection, and audit logs. Never let one tenant's data enter another's prompt or cache.

questions.q: How do you design caching for LLM applications?
questions.answer: Exact-match response cache for repeated identical requests; provider prompt caching for long shared prefixes; semantic cache (embedding similarity above a strict threshold) for near-duplicate questions where answers do not depend on the user; embedding cache during ingestion. Include model and prompt versions in cache keys and set TTLs so answers do not go stale.

questions.q: How do you route queries across multiple models?
questions.answer: Classify each request by difficulty, task type or required capability (a rules layer or a small classifier), send easy requests to a cheap fast model and hard ones to a stronger model, and escalate when a verifier or confidence check fails. Measure quality and cost per route.

questions.q: How do you migrate a product from one model to another?
questions.answer: Run both on the eval set, adjust prompts for the new model, shadow-test on live traffic, compare quality, latency and cost, roll out gradually behind a flag with rollback, and keep monitoring. Re-embed if the embedding model changes.

questions.q: Design a code-assistant feature for an IDE.
questions.answer: Context gathering (current file, related files via retrieval over the repo, recent edits), a low-latency model for inline completion and a stronger one for chat or multi-file edits, streaming, a sandbox for running tests, and acceptance-rate and edit-survival metrics. Respect repository permissions and keep secrets out of prompts.

questions.q: How do you monitor an LLM system in production?
questions.answer: Log each request with prompt version, model, tokens, latency, cost and outcome; trace multi-step calls; dashboards and alerts on error rate, p95 latency, cost spikes and quality signals; sample conversations for review; and track user feedback. Redact PII in logs.

questions.q: How do you reduce LLM inference cost?
questions.answer: Route easy requests to smaller models, shorten prompts, use prompt caching for shared prefixes, cache responses, cap output length, batch offline work (batch APIs are usually discounted), and for self-hosting use quantization and continuous batching. Track cost per successful task.

questions.q: How do you reduce latency?
questions.answer: Stream tokens, choose smaller or faster models for the first response, cut prompt length, parallelize retrieval and tool calls, cache, place servers near users, and use speculative decoding when self-hosting. Measure time to first token and total time separately.

questions.q: How do you handle provider rate limits and outages?
questions.answer: Retry transient errors with exponential backoff and jitter, respect retry-after headers, queue non-urgent work, spread load across keys or regions where allowed, and fail over to a secondary model or provider with a tested prompt.

questions.q: How do you handle PII in AI systems?
questions.answer: Minimize what is sent, detect and redact or tokenize PII before prompts and logs, check provider data-retention and training terms, encrypt at rest and in transit, apply retention limits, and support deletion requests. Test redaction recall; missed PII in logs is a common leak.

questions.q: What is model or data drift, and how do you detect it?
questions.answer: The input distribution, user behavior or the provider model itself changes, and quality shifts. Detect it by monitoring input statistics and topics, eval scores on sampled traffic, user feedback and outcome metrics over time, and by pinning model versions so upgrades are deliberate.

questions.q: What does red-teaming an AI system involve?
questions.answer: Deliberately attacking the system before release: jailbreaks, prompt injection through every input channel, data exfiltration, harmful content, tool misuse and bias. Use a threat model, both automated attack generation and human testers, record findings with severity, fix, and turn findings into regression tests.

questions.q: What are guardrails, and where do they sit?
questions.answer: Checks around the model: input checks (policy, injection signals, PII), output checks (policy, schema, groundedness, sensitive data), and action checks (tool permissions, confirmations). Keep them independent of the main prompt so one failure does not disable all protection, and measure their false positive rate.

questions.q: How do you measure and reduce bias in an LLM feature?
questions.answer: Define the harms relevant to your use case, build test sets that vary protected attributes while holding the task constant, compare outcomes and error rates across groups, and review qualitatively. Reduce with better data, prompt and policy changes, and human review for high-stakes decisions.

questions.q: How do you deploy prompt or model changes safely?
questions.answer: Treat them like code: review, offline evals in CI, feature flags, canary or percentage rollout with automated rollback on metric drops, and versioned configs so any response can be traced to the exact prompt and model.

questions.q: Implement retry with exponential backoff for an LLM API call.
questions.answer: Retry only transient failures (429, 5xx, timeouts), not 4xx validation errors. Wait base * 2^attempt plus random jitter, honor Retry-After, cap attempts and total time.

questions.q: Write a structure-aware text chunker.
questions.answer:
Split on headings and blank lines first, then pack paragraphs into chunks up to a token budget, with a small overlap, and never split inside code blocks.

Pass a real tokenizer's length function as count; len counts characters.

questions.q: Implement hybrid search with reciprocal rank fusion.
questions.answer: Run BM25 and vector search separately, then fuse by rank, which avoids normalizing incompatible scores.

questions.q: Parse and validate structured output from an LLM, with a repair retry.
questions.answer: Prefer the provider's schema mode when available; keep this as the safety net.

questions.q: Implement a token-bucket rate limiter for LLM calls.
questions.answer: Limit both requests and tokens per minute, because providers enforce both.

questions.q: Implement a minimal agent loop with tool calls and a step limit.
questions.answer: In production add argument validation, budgets, checkpointing and approval for side-effecting tools.

questions.q: Implement a conversation-history manager that fits a token budget.
questions.answer: Always keep the system prompt and the latest user turn; add earlier turns newest-first until the budget is reached; summarize what was dropped into one message.

questions.q: Write a small eval harness that compares two prompt versions.
questions.answer: Graders return 0 or 1 (exact match, schema valid, judge pass). Report per-case diffs so regressions are visible, and fix the random seed or temperature for repeatability.

questions.q: Walk me through the three financial statements.
questions.answer: The income statement shows revenue, expenses and net income over a period. The balance sheet shows assets, liabilities and shareholders’ equity at a point in time, and assets must equal liabilities plus equity. The cash flow statement starts with net income, adjusts for non-cash items and changes in working capital (cash flow from operations), then adds cash flow from investing and from financing, giving the net change in cash.
questions.follow_up: Which statement would you pick if you could only have one? A common answer is the cash flow statement, because it shows real cash generation, and you can roughly rebuild the rest with a beginning balance sheet.

questions.q: How do the three statements link together?
questions.answer: Net income from the income statement is the first line of the cash flow statement. Non-cash charges (such as depreciation) and changes in balance sheet working capital items adjust it to cash from operations; capital expenditures, debt and equity flows appear in investing and financing. The net change in cash updates cash on the balance sheet, and net income (less dividends) flows into retained earnings, which keeps the balance sheet balanced.

questions.q: If depreciation goes up by $10, walk me through the impact on all three statements.
questions.answer: Assume a 25% tax rate. Income statement: operating income and pre-tax income fall by $10; net income falls by $7.50. Cash flow statement: net income is down $7.50, but depreciation is a non-cash expense, so you add back $10; cash is up $2.50 (the tax saving). Balance sheet: cash +$2.50, net PP&E -$10, so total assets are down $7.50; retained earnings fall by $7.50, so liabilities plus equity are also down $7.50. It balances.

questions.q: What is the difference between cash-based and accrual-based accounting?
questions.answer: Accrual accounting records revenue when earned and expenses when incurred, regardless of when cash moves; it is required under US GAAP for most public companies. Cash accounting records transactions only when cash is received or paid. That gap is why the cash flow statement exists: it reconciles accrual-based net income back to cash.

questions.q: A company prepays $12M in rent for the year. Walk me through the impact.
questions.answer: At payment (25% tax rate): no income statement effect yet. Cash falls by $12M and a prepaid expense asset rises by $12M; on the cash flow statement the increase in prepaid expenses is a $12M use of cash in operating activities. As each month passes, $1M of rent expense is recognized and the prepaid balance falls by $1M. Over the full year: pre-tax income -$12M, net income -$9M; on the cash flow statement the $12M decline in prepaid expenses is added back, so that period’s operating cash flow is +$3M (the tax saving). Across both steps, cash is down $9M, prepaid is back to zero and retained earnings are down $9M.

questions.q: What is goodwill? How is it created?
questions.answer: Goodwill is the amount by which the purchase price of an acquired company exceeds the fair value of its identifiable net assets (after writing up assets and recognizing intangibles such as customer relationships and technology). It represents things like brand value, assembled workforce and expected synergies that cannot be separately identified. Under US GAAP it is not amortized for public companies; it is tested for impairment at least annually.

questions.q: How does a goodwill impairment affect the three statements?
questions.answer: Say a $100 impairment that is not tax-deductible (the usual case for goodwill from a stock deal). Income statement: a $100 impairment charge reduces pre-tax and net income by $100. Cash flow statement: net income -$100, add back the $100 non-cash charge, so cash is unchanged. Balance sheet: goodwill -$100 and retained earnings -$100. If the impairment were tax-deductible at 25%, net income would fall $75 and cash would rise $25.
questions.follow_up: Why is it not usually deductible? Goodwill from a stock purchase has no tax basis, unlike goodwill from an asset deal, which is amortized for US tax over 15 years.

questions.q: What is the difference between enterprise value and equity value?
questions.answer: Equity value is the value of the company’s shares to common shareholders: diluted shares outstanding times the share price. Enterprise value is the value of the core operating business to all capital providers (debt, preferred, noncontrolling interests and equity), excluding non-operating assets such as excess cash. Use EV with metrics available to all capital providers (revenue, EBITDA, EBIT, unlevered FCF) and equity value with metrics after interest (net income, EPS, levered FCF).

questions.q: Walk me through the enterprise value bridge.
questions.answer: Start with equity value (diluted shares times share price). Add debt, preferred stock and noncontrolling interests, plus other debt-like items if relevant (for example unfunded pension obligations, and lease liabilities when the metric excludes lease expense). Subtract cash and cash equivalents and non-operating assets such as equity-method investments. The result is enterprise value.

questions.q: Why do we add back minority interest in the EV bridge?
questions.answer: When a parent owns more than 50% of a subsidiary, it consolidates 100% of that subsidiary’s revenue and EBITDA even though it owns less than all of it. Adding the noncontrolling interest makes the numerator (EV) consistent with a denominator (EBITDA) that includes the whole subsidiary. Equity-method investments (under 50%) are subtracted for the opposite reason: their EBITDA is not consolidated.

questions.q: What is deferred revenue? Give an example.
questions.answer: Deferred revenue is cash received for goods or services not yet delivered; it is a liability until earned. Example: a customer pays $1,200 upfront for a 12-month software subscription. The company records $1,200 of deferred revenue and recognizes $100 of revenue each month as it delivers the service.

questions.q: Is deferred revenue a source or use of cash?
questions.answer: An increase in deferred revenue is a source of cash: the company has collected cash before recognizing revenue, so it appears as a positive working capital adjustment in cash flow from operations. A decrease is a use of cash.

questions.q: What is the difference between LIFO and FIFO? How does each affect the financial statements in an inflationary environment?
questions.answer: FIFO expenses the oldest inventory costs first; LIFO expenses the newest. With rising prices, LIFO gives higher cost of goods sold, lower net income and lower taxes (so higher cash flow) and a lower ending inventory balance; FIFO gives lower COGS, higher net income, higher taxes and an inventory balance closer to current cost. LIFO is allowed under US GAAP but not IFRS.

questions.q: How do you calculate free cash flow to firm (FCFF)?
questions.answer: FCFF (unlevered free cash flow) = EBIT x (1 - tax rate) + depreciation and amortization - capital expenditures - increase in net working capital. Equivalently, cash flow from operations + after-tax interest expense - capital expenditures. It is the cash available to all capital providers, before debt payments.

questions.q: How do you calculate free cash flow to equity (FCFE)?
questions.answer: FCFE (levered free cash flow) = net income + D&A - capital expenditures - increase in net working capital + net borrowing (new debt minus repayments). Equivalently, FCFF - interest x (1 - tax rate) + net borrowing. It is the cash available to equity holders and is discounted at the cost of equity.

questions.q: What is stock-based compensation? Why do some people add it back in FCFF?
questions.answer: Stock-based compensation pays employees in shares or options instead of cash. It is a non-cash expense, so it is added back on the cash flow statement. It is still a real cost to shareholders because it dilutes them. If you add SBC back to free cash flow, you must reflect the future dilution in the share count; the more conservative approach is to treat it as a cash-like expense and not add it back.

questions.q: A company issues $100M in debt to buy back stock. Walk me through the impact on all three statements.
questions.answer: At the transaction: debt +$100M and shareholders’ equity -$100M (treasury stock), so the balance sheet still balances; on the cash flow statement, financing shows +$100M from debt and -$100M for the buyback, so cash is unchanged; no income statement effect. Going forward: interest expense rises (at 6%, $6M pre-tax, $4.5M after tax at 25%), net income falls, but share count falls too, so EPS can rise if the after-tax cost of debt is below the earnings yield on the repurchased shares.

questions.q: What is a deferred tax asset? A deferred tax liability? Give examples of each.
questions.answer: A deferred tax liability arises when pre-tax income on the financial statements is higher than taxable income because of a timing difference, so more tax will be paid later. Example: accelerated depreciation for tax and straight-line for the books, or asset write-ups in a stock acquisition that are not deductible for tax. A deferred tax asset is the reverse: taxable income is higher now, or a future tax deduction exists. Examples: net operating loss carryforwards, and warranty or bad-debt reserves expensed in the books before they are tax-deductible.

questions.q: Why would two companies with identical pre-tax income have different tax rates?
questions.answer: Different geographic mix (tax rates differ by country and state), tax credits such as R&D credits, use of net operating losses, permanent differences (non-deductible expenses, tax-exempt income), changes in valuation allowances, and one-time items such as settlements with tax authorities.

questions.q: What is working capital? How does an increase in working capital affect cash flow?
questions.answer: Working capital is current assets minus current liabilities. For valuation, bankers usually use operating working capital, which excludes cash and debt (accounts receivable + inventory + prepaid expenses - accounts payable - accrued expenses - deferred revenue). An increase in operating working capital means more cash is tied up in the business, so it reduces cash flow; a decrease releases cash.

questions.q: What is the difference between capitalizing and expensing?
questions.answer: Capitalizing records a cost as an asset on the balance sheet and expenses it over time through depreciation or amortization; it is used when the item provides benefit over more than one year (e.g. equipment). Expensing records it immediately on the income statement (e.g. salaries, rent). Capitalizing makes current-period income higher and puts the cash outflow in investing rather than operating activities.

questions.q: A company changes from straight-line to accelerated depreciation. Impact?
questions.answer: Accelerated depreciation means more expense in early years and less later; total depreciation over the asset’s life is the same. Early years: higher depreciation, lower pre-tax and net income; assuming the method applies for tax purposes, taxes fall, so cash flow rises (by depreciation change times the tax rate), PP&E falls faster and retained earnings fall. Later years reverse. If only the book method changes and tax depreciation does not, cash taxes are unchanged and a deferred tax effect appears instead.

questions.q: How do operating leases appear on the financial statements under ASC 842?
questions.answer: Under ASC 842, an operating lease puts a right-of-use asset and a lease liability on the balance sheet. On the income statement, there is a single straight-line lease cost within operating expenses (unlike a finance lease, which shows amortization and interest separately). Payments are in cash flow from operations. Because lease cost stays inside US GAAP EBITDA, bankers usually do not add operating lease liabilities to enterprise value; under IFRS 16, where lease cost sits in depreciation and interest, lease liabilities are usually added.

questions.q: A company sells an asset for more than book value. Walk me through the impact.
questions.answer: Say an asset with a $80 book value sells for $100 and the tax rate is 25%. Income statement: $20 gain, net income +$15. Cash flow statement: net income +$15, subtract the $20 gain in operating activities (it is non-operating), and record $100 of proceeds in investing activities: cash +$95. Balance sheet: cash +$95, PP&E -$80, total assets +$15; retained earnings +$15. It balances.

questions.q: What is diluted shares outstanding and how do you calculate it using the treasury stock method?
questions.answer: Diluted shares include the effect of options, warrants, RSUs and convertibles. Under the treasury stock method, assume in-the-money options are exercised and the company uses the exercise proceeds to buy back shares at the current price. Example: 100M basic shares, 10M options with a $10 strike, share price $20. Proceeds are $100M, which buys back 5M shares, so net new shares are 5M and diluted shares are 105M. Out-of-the-money options are excluded.

questions.q: Walk me through a DCF.
questions.answer: Project the company’s unlevered free cash flows, usually for 5 to 10 years, from revenue, margins, taxes, capex and working capital. Calculate a terminal value at the end of the projection period with the Gordon Growth method or an exit multiple. Discount the cash flows and the terminal value to today at the weighted average cost of capital. The sum is enterprise value; subtract net debt and other claims to get equity value, and divide by diluted shares to get value per share.
questions.follow_up: why use unlevered free cash flow? Because the discount rate (WACC) reflects all capital providers, so the cash flow must be before debt payments too.

questions.q: What is WACC and how do you calculate it?
questions.answer: WACC is the blended required return of all capital providers: WACC = E/(D+E) x cost of equity + D/(D+E) x cost of debt x (1 - tax rate), plus a preferred-stock term if relevant. Use market values or a target capital structure for the weights. Cost of debt is the current yield or borrowing rate, after tax because interest is tax-deductible.

questions.q: How do you calculate cost of equity?
questions.answer: With the Capital Asset Pricing Model: cost of equity = risk-free rate + levered beta x equity risk premium. Some practitioners add a size or company-specific premium. The risk-free rate is usually a long-term government bond yield matching the currency of the cash flows.

questions.q: What beta would you use for a private company?
questions.answer: A private company has no trading history, so use comparable public companies. Take each peer’s levered beta, unlever it to remove its capital structure (unlevered beta = levered beta / (1 + (1 - tax rate) x debt/equity)), take the median, then relever it at the private company’s target capital structure.

questions.q: What is the terminal value and how do you calculate it?
questions.answer: Terminal value captures the value of cash flows beyond the projection period. Gordon Growth: final-year free cash flow x (1 + long-term growth rate) / (discount rate - growth rate). Exit multiple: final-year EBITDA (or another metric) x an exit multiple from comparable companies. Discount it back to today from the end of the projection period. It is often the majority of a DCF’s value, so sensitivity tables on its inputs matter.

questions.q: Gordon Growth vs. Exit Multiple for terminal value: when do you use each?
questions.answer: Exit multiple is common in banking because it ties to market valuations and to how buyers think about exits. Gordon Growth suits mature, stable businesses and is preferred when there are few good comparables or when market multiples are distorted. Best practice is to cross-check: compute the growth rate implied by your exit multiple and the multiple implied by your growth rate. The long-term growth rate should not exceed long-run nominal GDP growth.

questions.q: A company has negative free cash flow for the next 5 years. Can you still do a DCF?
questions.answer: Yes. Extend the projection period until cash flows turn positive and reach a steady state, then calculate terminal value. The result will be heavily dependent on terminal value and assumptions, so use a higher discount rate if risk is higher, run scenarios, and cross-check with comparable companies and transactions.

questions.q: Walk me through how you would build a comparable companies analysis.
questions.answer: Select a peer set of similar companies, gather their financials (historical LTM and projected NTM or forward-year figures) and share data, calculate equity value and enterprise value for each, compute multiples such as EV/Revenue, EV/EBITDA and P/E, then look at the median and the 25th to 75th percentile range. Apply that range to the target’s corresponding metrics to get an implied valuation range.

questions.q: How do you select comparable companies?
questions.answer: Start with industry and business model, then filter by size (revenue or market cap), growth, margins, geography and end markets. You want companies investors would see as substitutes. Usually 5 to 15 peers, adjusted when the closest names have unusual circumstances (pending acquisition, distress).

questions.q: Why do we use NTM multiples vs. LTM multiples?
questions.answer: Valuation is forward-looking: the market prices expected earnings, so NTM multiples reflect consensus expectations and smooth one-time items in historical results. They matter most for fast-growing or changing companies. LTM multiples use actual reported results and are more objective when forecasts are unreliable or unavailable.

questions.q: Why do precedent transactions typically give higher valuations than comparable companies?
questions.answer: Because acquirers pay a control premium over the market price to gain control of the target, and they often pay part of the expected synergies. Precedent multiples also reflect market conditions at the time of each deal, which may differ from today.

questions.q: If you could only use one valuation methodology, which would you choose?
questions.answer: There is no single right answer; the interviewer wants your reasoning. A common answer is a DCF, because it values the company’s own cash flows and does not depend on whether the market is mispricing peers, as long as cash flows are reasonably predictable. Another defensible answer is trading comparables, because they reflect what investors pay today and rely on fewer assumptions. Pick one and give the trade-off.

questions.q: Which gives the highest valuation: DCF, comps, or precedent transactions?
questions.answer: There is no fixed rule. Precedent transactions often come out highest because they include control premiums. A DCF has the widest range because it is very sensitive to assumptions. Trading comparables often come out lower than precedents. The answer depends on the market environment and the assumptions.

questions.q: When would you not use a DCF?
questions.answer: When cash flows are unpredictable or there is no reasonable way to project them, such as an early-stage startup. For banks and insurers, a standard unlevered DCF does not work because debt and interest are part of operations, so use a dividend discount model or residual income model instead. In distressed situations, liquidation or recovery analysis may be more relevant.

questions.q: A company’s DCF gives $50/share but it trades at $30. What could explain this?
questions.answer: The market may see risks your model does not, your projections may be too optimistic, your discount rate may be too low, or your terminal assumptions too aggressive. Or the market may be mispricing the stock temporarily, for example because of short-term sentiment or limited information. Sense-check your assumptions against consensus estimates and comparable multiples before concluding the stock is undervalued.

questions.q: How does a decrease in WACC affect the DCF output?
questions.answer: A lower WACC increases the present value of future cash flows and the terminal value, so enterprise value goes up. With the Gordon Growth method the effect is magnified because value depends on the spread between the discount rate and the growth rate.

questions.q: What is the equity risk premium and what value do you use?
questions.answer: The equity risk premium is the extra return investors expect from equities over the risk-free rate. There is no single correct number; US practitioners commonly use a figure in roughly the 4% to 6% range, sourced from a house view, historical averages, or implied-premium estimates such as those published by Aswath Damodaran or advisory firms. Say what source you use and why.

questions.q: How do you value a company with no revenue?
questions.answer: Use methods that do not rely on current profits: a DCF with a long projection period and scenario or probability weighting, comparable companies on forward revenue or operating metrics (users, subscribers), recent private funding rounds or precedent transactions, and for drug developers a risk-adjusted NPV based on clinical success probabilities. Asset or liquidation value can set a floor.

questions.q: What is a sum-of-the-parts valuation?
questions.answer: A sum-of-the-parts values each business segment separately with the method and multiples appropriate to it, then adds them, subtracts unallocated corporate costs (capitalized) and net debt, and sometimes applies a conglomerate discount. It is used for diversified companies whose segments have very different growth, margins or peer groups, and to test break-up or spin-off value.

questions.q: How do you value a cyclical company?
questions.answer: Avoid valuing a cyclical company on peak or trough earnings. Normalize: use mid-cycle or average EBITDA and margins across a full cycle, apply multiples to normalized figures, and in a DCF project a full cycle so the terminal year is not at a peak. Cross-check with multiples of peers at a similar point in the cycle.

questions.q: What are calendarized financials and why do they matter for comps?
questions.answer: Calendarization adjusts financial results of companies with different fiscal year-ends to the same calendar period so multiples are comparable. Example: for a company with a June fiscal year-end, calendar year 2026 = 6/12 of fiscal year ending June 2026 + 6/12 of fiscal year ending June 2027.

questions.q: How do convertible bonds affect the EV calculation?
questions.answer: Check whether the convertible is in the money (share price above the conversion price). If it is, treat it as equity: add the shares it converts into to the diluted share count (if-converted method) and do not count it as debt. If it is out of the money, treat it as debt in the EV bridge. Do not count it in both places.

questions.q: A company has $500M in cash. Does all of it get subtracted in the EV bridge?
questions.answer: Not necessarily. You subtract cash that is not needed to run the business. Some analysts keep a minimum operating cash balance in the business, and restricted or trapped cash, or cash held abroad that would be taxed on repatriation, may be adjusted. Whatever you choose, stay consistent across the target and its comparables.

questions.q: What is unlevered free cash flow and how does it differ from levered FCF?
questions.answer: Unlevered free cash flow is cash flow before interest and debt payments, available to all capital providers; discount it at WACC to get enterprise value. Levered free cash flow is after interest and mandatory debt repayments, available only to equity holders; discount it at the cost of equity to get equity value.

questions.q: If you raise the discount rate in a DCF by 1%, does the value go up or down? By approximately how much?
questions.answer: Value goes down. The size depends on the inputs, especially the gap between the discount rate and the terminal growth rate. Example with Gordon Growth only: at a 10% discount rate and 2% growth, terminal value is proportional to 1/0.08; at 11% it is 1/0.09, about 11% lower. A one-point change commonly moves DCF value by roughly 10% to 15%, which is why bankers show sensitivity tables.

questions.q: Walk me through a merger model.
questions.answer: Set the purchase price and form of consideration (cash, stock, debt). Project both companies’ income statements. Combine them and adjust for foregone interest on cash used, interest on new debt, new shares issued, amortization of new intangibles, and synergies. Compute pro forma EPS and compare it with the buyer’s standalone EPS to see accretion or dilution. A fuller model also builds the pro forma balance sheet with purchase price allocation and goodwill.

questions.q: What is accretion/dilution?
questions.answer: A deal is accretive if the combined company’s pro forma EPS is higher than the buyer’s standalone EPS, and dilutive if it is lower. It is a shorthand that markets watch, but it is not the same as value creation; a dilutive deal can still create value and vice versa.

questions.q: In an all-stock deal, what determines if it is accretive or dilutive?
questions.answer: Compare the buyer’s P/E with the P/E it pays for the seller. If the buyer’s P/E is higher than the purchase P/E for the target, the deal is accretive, ignoring synergies and other adjustments. Put differently, the cost of stock (the buyer’s earnings yield, 1/P/E) is lower than the yield of the earnings acquired.
questions.follow_up: for a mixed deal, compare the weighted cost of acquisition (after-tax cost of debt, foregone interest on cash, buyer’s earnings yield for stock) with the seller’s earnings yield at the purchase price.

questions.q: Why might a company do a dilutive acquisition?
questions.answer: Because accretion/dilution is a short-term EPS measure. The buyer may expect synergies that ramp up later, the target may grow faster than the buyer, it may add strategic capabilities, markets or technology, or it may be defensive against a competitor. Dilution in year one can turn into accretion in later years.

questions.q: What are synergies? Types and typical ranges?
questions.answer: Synergies are the extra value from combining two companies. Cost synergies come from eliminating overlapping costs: headcount, facilities, procurement and systems. Revenue synergies come from cross-selling, pricing and access to new channels or markets. There are also financial synergies such as tax benefits or cheaper financing. Cost synergies are more predictable, so investors and bankers usually discount revenue synergies more heavily. Sanity-check estimates as a percentage of the target’s cost base and against precedent deals.

questions.q: Why do most acquisitions fail to deliver expected synergies?
questions.answer: Integration is harder than planned (systems, culture, key people leaving), revenue synergies assume customer behavior that does not happen, customers and employees leave during uncertainty, one-time integration costs are underestimated, and the buyer overpays, so even achieved synergies do not cover the premium.

questions.q: What is a fairness opinion?
questions.answer: A fairness opinion is a letter from a financial advisor to a company’s board stating that the consideration in a transaction is fair, from a financial point of view, to the company’s shareholders. It is supported by valuation analyses (DCF, comps, precedents) and helps the board show it made an informed decision. It is not a statement that the price is the best obtainable.

questions.q: What is a go-shop provision?
questions.answer: A go-shop clause lets the target actively solicit competing offers for a set period after signing a merger agreement, often around 30 to 60 days, usually with a lower break-up fee for a deal signed during that window. It is common when the target negotiated with one buyer without a broad auction, and it helps the board satisfy its duty to seek the best value.

questions.q: What is a MAC clause?
questions.answer: A material adverse change (or material adverse effect) clause lets a buyer walk away if something seriously harms the target between signing and closing. It is heavily negotiated, with carve-outs for general economic, market or industry conditions. Delaware courts set a high bar; Akorn v. Fresenius (2018) was the first time the Delaware Court of Chancery found an MAE allowing a buyer to terminate.

questions.q: Cash vs. stock vs. mixed consideration: trade-offs?
questions.answer: Cash gives the seller certainty and full exit, is usually taxable to the seller, and requires the buyer to have cash or raise debt. Stock shares risk and upside with the seller, can be tax-deferred, avoids new debt, but dilutes the buyer’s shareholders and the value fluctuates until closing. Buyers tend to use stock when they think their shares are richly valued; mixed consideration balances these trade-offs.

questions.q: What is a reverse merger?
questions.answer: A reverse merger is when a private company merges with an existing public company (often a shell with little operations) so the private company’s owners take control and the company becomes public without a traditional IPO. It is faster and cheaper than an IPO but usually raises less capital and can carry diligence and reputational risk.

questions.q: What is an earnout and when is it used?
questions.answer: An earnout is part of the purchase price paid later only if the target hits agreed milestones, such as revenue, EBITDA or regulatory approval. It bridges a valuation gap between buyer and seller, especially for high-growth or uncertain businesses (for example biotech or early-stage tech). Downsides: disputes over measurement and less buyer freedom to integrate.

questions.q: Name three anti-takeover defenses.
questions.answer: A poison pill (shareholder rights plan) lets existing holders buy shares at a discount if an acquirer crosses an ownership threshold, diluting the acquirer. A staggered board means only part of the board is elected each year, slowing a takeover. Other defenses: a white knight (friendly alternative buyer), dual-class shares, and golden parachutes.

questions.q: What is the role of the sell-side advisor vs. the buy-side advisor?
questions.answer: The sell-side advisor represents the company or owner being sold: prepares the materials, identifies and contacts buyers, runs the auction and negotiates to maximize value and certainty. The buy-side advisor represents the acquirer: identifies targets, values them, advises on bid strategy, structure and financing, and helps negotiate. Both typically help with fairness opinions or financing as needed.

questions.q: What factors influence the premium paid in an acquisition?
questions.answer: Synergies the buyer expects, competition among bidders, the target’s growth and strategic value, the buyer’s ability to pay and financing conditions, the target’s recent share price and how much speculation is already in it, market conditions, and governance factors such as shareholder support or defenses.

questions.q: Walk me through a sell-side M&A process.
questions.answer: Preparation: valuation, buyer list, teaser and confidential information memorandum (CIM), data room. First round: buyers sign NDAs, receive the CIM and submit non-binding indications of interest. Second round: selected buyers get management presentations and data room access and submit final bids with a markup of the purchase agreement. Then negotiation, signing, regulatory approvals and closing. A full process commonly takes several months.

questions.q: What is the difference between an asset deal and a stock deal?
questions.answer: In an asset deal the buyer purchases specific assets and assumes only chosen liabilities; it gets a step-up in tax basis, so it can depreciate and amortize the asset write-ups (including goodwill, amortized over 15 years for US tax). A C-corporation seller may face double taxation. In a stock deal the buyer acquires the shares and all liabilities; there is generally no tax step-up. Buyers usually prefer asset deals and sellers stock deals. A Section 338(h)(10) or 336(e) election can treat a stock deal as an asset deal for tax purposes in certain situations.

questions.q: How do you calculate goodwill in an acquisition?
questions.answer: Goodwill = purchase price for the equity - fair value of the target’s identifiable net assets. In practice: purchase equity value - target’s book value of equity (excluding existing goodwill) - write-ups of assets including new identifiable intangibles + any deferred tax liability created by the write-ups.

questions.q: What is purchase price allocation?
questions.answer: Purchase price allocation assigns the purchase price to the fair values of the target’s acquired assets and assumed liabilities, including identifiable intangibles (customer relationships, technology, trade names). Any excess is goodwill. It determines future depreciation and amortization, which affects the pro forma income statement.

questions.q: A company wants to acquire a target but cannot afford to pay cash. What options does it have?
questions.answer: Pay in stock, raise debt (bank loans or bonds), issue new equity or a hybrid such as convertibles, use seller financing (a seller note) or an earnout to defer part of the price, partner with a private equity firm or co-investor, sell non-core assets first, or buy a partial stake or form a joint venture.

questions.q: Walk me through an LBO model.
questions.answer: A private equity firm buys a company using a large amount of debt and some equity. Steps: set the purchase price and sources and uses (debt and sponsor equity versus purchase price and fees); project the company’s cash flows; use free cash flow to pay interest and repay debt; assume an exit after about 3 to 7 years at an exit multiple; subtract remaining net debt to get exit equity value; calculate IRR and MOIC on the sponsor’s equity.

questions.q: What makes a good LBO candidate?
questions.answer: Stable, predictable cash flows to service debt; limited capital expenditure needs; a strong market position; room to improve operations or grow; a reasonable purchase price; assets that support borrowing; a capable management team; and a clear path to exit through a sale or IPO.

questions.q: What are the three ways PE firms create value?
questions.answer: EBITDA growth (revenue growth and margin improvement), multiple expansion (selling at a higher multiple than the purchase multiple) and debt paydown (deleveraging, which increases the equity’s share of enterprise value). Leverage itself magnifies returns on all three.

questions.q: Do a paper LBO: 10x entry, $200M EBITDA, 6x debt, 5% growth, exit 10x in 5 years.
questions.answer: Entry: 10x x $200M = $2,000M enterprise value; debt 6x = $1,200M; equity $800M (ignore fees). EBITDA in year 5 = $200M x 1.05^5, about $255M. Exit at 10x = about $2,553M. If no debt is repaid, exit equity = $2,553M - $1,200M = $1,353M, MOIC about 1.7x, IRR about 11%. If, say, $300M of debt is repaid from free cash flow, exit equity is about $1,653M, MOIC about 2.1x, IRR about 15 to 16%.

questions.q: What is IRR? What is MOIC? How do they relate?
questions.answer: IRR is the discount rate that makes the net present value of the equity cash flows zero, so it accounts for timing. MOIC (multiple on invested capital) is total value returned divided by equity invested, with no time element. For a single entry and exit, IRR = MOIC^(1/years) - 1, so the same MOIC over a shorter hold means a higher IRR.

questions.q: Which creates more value: 1 turn of multiple expansion or 1 turn of additional leverage?
questions.answer: It depends on the numbers, so show it. One turn of exit multiple adds one turn times exit EBITDA of value directly to equity. One more turn of leverage reduces the equity check; it raises returns only if the business earns more than the after-tax cost of the extra debt and can service it, and it raises risk. Example: $100M EBITDA, 10x entry and exit, 5x debt, no growth or paydown: equity in $500M, out $500M. Exit at 11x: out $600M, +20%. Use 6x debt instead: equity in $400M, out $400M, still 1.0x, because nothing grew. In a no-growth case, multiple expansion helps more.

questions.q: What is a dividend recapitalization?
questions.answer: A dividend recapitalization is when a portfolio company raises new debt and uses it to pay a dividend to its private equity owners. It returns capital early and raises IRR without selling the company, but increases leverage and default risk.

questions.q: Why can PE firms pay higher multiples than strategic buyers in some situations?
questions.answer: Normally strategic buyers can pay more because of synergies. A sponsor can pay more when debt is cheap and plentiful, when it sees operational improvements the market undervalues, when it has a platform that creates add-on synergies, or when a strategic buyer is constrained by its own share price, balance sheet, antitrust concerns or EPS dilution.

questions.q: What is PIK (payment in kind) interest?
questions.answer: Payment-in-kind interest is not paid in cash; it is added to the principal, so the debt balance grows. It preserves cash for the borrower but carries a higher rate and compounds. In the model, PIK interest reduces net income but is added back on the cash flow statement as a non-cash expense.

questions.q: What debt covenants are common in LBOs?
questions.answer: Maintenance covenants require ongoing tests, such as a maximum total leverage ratio (debt/EBITDA) or minimum interest or fixed-charge coverage.
